A process is a running program: the kernel gives it a process ID, the PID, its own memory, and a table of open files starting with stdin, stdout and stderr. A signal is a notification the kernel delivers to interrupt whatever that process is doing, and pressing Ctrl+C sends one specific signal,
, to every process in the foreground group. Left uncaught,
's default action terminates the process at once. When any process ends, the kernel holds its exit status, a number from 0 to 255, until the parent collects it with
. A status of 0 means success and anything else is a chosen failure, except that a process a signal killed never chose one, so the shell reports 128 plus the signal's number instead: 130 for
The problem this creates is that the default action gives a program no chance to save anything: a log to flush, a file to close, loses that chance the moment

The mechanism is a handler that does the smallest thing possible: set a flag, nothing else. That flag needs a type a handler may safely touch with no ordering against the main loop, such as an atomic, because a signal can interrupt a function like

that already holds an internal lock, and calling back into one from inside the handler can deadlock or corrupt the heap. The main loop reads the flag in ordinary code, breaks out, does the real cleanup there, and exits with whatever status it chooses. This is how

subs.title: Processes, ps, top, kill, signals, exit status

c.v: Start a process, stop it with a signal, and see what the shell reports:

blocks.text:
sleep 100 &                     # start in the background; $! holds its process ID
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p $!   # its ID, its parent's ID, its state (S: sleeping) and its command
kill -TERM $!                   # send SIGTERM, the polite request to stop
wait $!; echo $?                # prints 143
false; echo $?                  # prints 1

An exit status is a number from 0 to 255. 0 means success, and any other value is a failure whose meaning the program chooses, such as the 1 from
. A process killed by a signal never returns a status of its own, so the shell reports 128 plus the signal number. SIGTERM is signal 15, which is where the 143 comes from.

c.v: A handler for SIGSEGV or SIGABRT runs in a process that is already broken, so there is little it can do safely. Leave those two to their default action and read the core dump or the sanitizer report instead. The sanitizers themselves don't end the process with a signal. A GCC 13 build with AddressSanitizer exits with status 1 after its report, and so does UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer when it is built with
gives 134, which is 128 plus the 6 of SIGABRT.
To look at running processes and what they use, these commands cover most needs:

blocks.text:
ps -ef                                   # every process, with its PID and its parent's PID
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,rss,cmd -p 1234      # one process: state, resident memory in KB, command
pgrep -a talker                          # find processes by name
top                                      # live CPU and memory use; press M to sort by memory
kill -TERM 1234                          # ask a process to stop (kill sends SIGTERM by default)
kill -INT 1234                           # the same signal as Ctrl+C
kill -KILL 1234                          # stop it at once; it gets no chance to clean up
cat /proc/1234/status                    # the kernel's view: state, threads, memory
journalctl -k | grep -i "out of memory"  # was it killed by the out-of-memory killer?

c.v: Every ROS 2 node is a process, so all of this applies to your robot. When you press Ctrl+C in a terminal running

, the terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground process group, which includes every node launch started. Launch sends SIGINT itself only when it shuts down for another reason, or runs non-interactive. Either way, launch then sends SIGTERM to a node that is still running 5 seconds later, and one that is still running 5 seconds after that gets SIGKILL, which it cannot catch. These are the defaults of the launch settings
installs handlers for both SIGINT and SIGTERM, and they only tell the node to shut down. So a C++ node whose loop never checks
survives both signals, holds up shutdown for 10 seconds, and is then killed with SIGKILL without cleaning up.

The flag is a global, and it has to be. A handler receives only the signal number, so whatever it touches must be reachable without an argument. This is the one exception to the rule against global mutable state (Core Guidelines

subs.title: Zombie and orphan processes; unsafe work in signal handlers

c.v: A child that has exited stays in the process table until its parent collects its status with

. It uses no memory, but it keeps its PID. A long-running parent that starts children and never waits for them leaks PIDs, and eventually the system can't start new processes. The parent has to wait for each child, directly or from a SIGCHLD handler that sets a flag.
When the parent dies first, the child becomes an
. PID 1 adopts it, or a "subreaper" such as systemd does, and collects its status when it ends. That is harmless, but it means killing a launcher doesn't necessarily stop the processes it started.
A signal can arrive in the middle of any function, including
, which hold internal locks. If the handler then calls one of those functions, the process can deadlock or corrupt its heap. That is why a handler may only call
are all unsafe. This handler is wrong in three ways, and the

writes through the same locked stdio buffer as

SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can't be caught at all, so no clean-up code runs when they arrive. Design for that. For example, write results to a temporary file and
it into place when it is complete, so a killed process never leaves a half-written file behind.
